Bushido. Literally the way of the warrior, the ethical and moral code governing the conduct of samurai in feudal Japan. Synthesizing elements of Buddhism, Shinto, and Confucian philosophy, bushido emphasized loyalty, honor, martial skill, and readiness for death. Though formalized as a philosophical system primarily during the Edo Period from 1603 to 1868, it has become central to Japanese identity and continues to influence Japanese culture, aesthetics, and values.

The name combines bushi, meaning warrior, and do, meaning way or path, reflecting a philosophical rather than merely practical code of conduct. Bushido emerged during the feudal period but was systematized and codified intellectually during the Edo Period, when samurai had transitioned from active warriors to administrative bureaucrats.

Central virtues included loyalty to one's lord, called daimyo, honor above life itself, martial proficiency, and readiness to commit seppuku, ritual suicide, rather than face dishonor. Bushido was influenced by Confucian emphasis on hierarchy, duty, and filial piety; Buddhist acceptance of death and impermanence; and Shinto reverence for the sacred and the warrior's spiritual purification. The code prescribed aesthetic refinement alongside martial skill. The ideal samurai practiced calligraphy, poetry, and tea ceremony as expressions of inner cultivation and spiritual discipline.

Bushido valued decisiveness, emotional restraint, and stoicism. Fear and hesitation were seen as dishonorable. Death in service was preferable to living with shame. Decline began with the Meiji Restoration in 1868, which abolished the samurai class and modernized Japan's military. Bushido survived as a cultural ideal and influenced modern Japanese nationalism. Later, it was invoked and distorted during World War Two to justify kamikaze pilots and militaristic expansionism. Postwar interpretations have emphasized its philosophical and ethical dimensions.
